title: Big churches and house churches
hook: Christians gather in stadiums and in living rooms

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nehemiah, and a cathedral rebuilt where a swimming pool had been. Your line was rebuilt. What stone did you lay? Day nine hundred eighty-four.

Three thousand. Then, two or three. Both numbers are in the New Testament, and both describe a church. On a Sunday you can find each shape. An arena: a full parking lot, a band on a stage, lyrics on screens the size of houses, a crowd you can't see the end of. And a living room: a sagging couch, two kitchen chairs, a pot of soup on the stove for after. Someone reads a psalm. Someone else admits a hard week. The people in both rooms would call it church. Today, big churches and house churches.

Big or small? The question goes back to the church's earliest pages, and the Bible doesn't pick a side. In Acts, on the day of Pentecost, Peter preaches to a crowd in Jerusalem, and in the King James Bible: "the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls." A crowd, in a single day. But a few lines later, here's how those same people lived: "continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart." The temple courts and the kitchen table, both, daily. When Paul writes his letters, he sends greetings to churches that meet in people's homes: "Likewise greet the church that is in their house." The Greek word behind church, ekklesia, means an assembly, a gathering. It fits a crowd, and it fits a couch. Today the two shapes live side by side. Big churches can put on worship that lifts a whole arena, run food banks, and give a newcomer a seat where nobody notices them yet. House churches can know every name, notice who's missing, and carry each other's groceries. Each has its critics, and its defenders, and some big churches split into small home groups during the week to get both. Under all of it sits a promise Jesus made in Matthew about the smallest gathering of all: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Two or three. Read that way, God doesn't wait for a crowd.
screen: `IN THE TEMPLE, AND FROM HOUSE TO HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather your two or three. If someone is with you right now, you can do this together. If not, do it in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind two or three people you would want in that living room. Not the impressive ones. The ones you'd let see a hard week. Picture them on the couch. Notice who came to mind first, and who you're surprised to miss. If you pray, you can pray for each of them by name, or pray with them later, even by phone. If you don't, simply hold them, one at a time, with good will. The bell holds the time.
Ekklesia. The New Testament word for church, an assembly that fits a crowd of thousands or a gathering in someone's house.
Your line: where two or three. Today, gather two or three, for a meal, a walk, a call, and if you pray, pray together, even briefly. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Christians gather in congregations of every size, from large churches with several services each weekend to small groups meeting in homes, and some large churches organize their members into weekly home groups for prayer and Bible study.

original.note: Greek: an assembly, a gathering — the New Testament word for church, used for a city's believers and for a house.

trapdoor: what you thought: real church means a building with a steeple.
what it means: Christians gather in arenas and in living rooms, and both count as church.
what a scholar hears: Acts 2:41 and 2:46, a crowd and house to house from the start, and ekklesia, a word for any assembly.

notes: 'three thousand' is stated because Acts 2:41 says it directly (claims rule satisfied).
'ekklesia means an assembly, a gathering': standard lexicon meaning; no etymology ('called out') given. Confirm.

'Christians read that line as saying God doesn't wait for a crowd' is a general reading of Matthew 18:20; soften to 'some Christians' if needed. The verse's context (church discipline, 18:15–20) is not discussed.
Strengths of big and house churches named without ranking; 'some big churches split into small home groups' is general; confirm.
